ideas.title: Aspect-Aware Evidence Gathering for Agentic Literature Review
ideas.research_question: Does integrating aspect-based retrieval (S3) into PaperQA2's evidence-gathering stage (S1) improve precision and recall on multi-faceted scientific questions compared to the baseline single-stage retrieval?
ideas.mechanism: Replace PaperQA2's (S1) retrieval step with the two-stage aspect-based pipeline from S3, decomposing each query into motivation, method, and result aspects before evidence gathering. The LLM reranker in S1 then operates over aspect-partitioned candidate sets, and the unanswerability signal from S3 propagates to PaperQA2's answer generation to flag underspecified queries.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Run the modified pipeline on the same literature QA benchmark used in S1, measuring F1, precision, recall, and unanswerable-question detection accuracy against the original PaperQA2 baseline and human PhD experts.

ideas.title: Novelty-Validated Overgenerate-and-Rerank for Scientific Hypothesis Generation
ideas.research_question: Does grounding the reranking stage of an LLM ideation agent (S2) with aspect-based novelty validation (S3) increase the proportion of top-ranked ideas that are both highly novel and verifiably non-redundant with existing literature?
ideas.mechanism: After the ideation agent (S2) overproduces candidate hypotheses, each candidate is passed through the S3 two-stage aspect-based retrieval pipeline to retrieve contradicting or supporting literature and compute a novelty score. Ideas flagged as unanswerable (no relevant prior work found) receive a novelty bonus; ideas with high overlap are penalized. The reranker (S2) incorporates these signals alongside its existing criteria.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Blind human NLP expert ratings of novelty and feasibility for top-k ideas produced with vs. without S3-based novelty filtering, using the same evaluation protocol as S2, measuring win rate and average novelty score.

ideas.title: Self-Improving Research Ideation via Agentic Literature Grounding
ideas.research_question: Can an LLM ideation agent (S2) that uses a PaperQA2-style agentic retriever (S1) for evidence gathering and novelty checking—rather than a static RAG index—produce ideas rated as more grounded and novel than those from a static-retrieval ideation baseline?
ideas.mechanism: Replace the static retrieval component of the S2 ideation agent with PaperQA2's (S1) agentic loop: citation traversal, dynamic paper search, and LLM reranking. For each overgenerated candidate idea, the agent runs a PaperQA2 query to gather supporting and contradicting evidence, then passes retrieved evidence and aspect-level novelty signals (S3) into the overgenerate-and-rerank scoring step (S2).
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Compare blind expert novelty and accuracy ratings for ideas produced by the fully agentic pipeline (S1+S2+S3) vs. a static-RAG ideation baseline (S2 alone) on a held-out set of NLP research prompts, reporting mean novelty score, grounding accuracy, and rate of hallucinated citations.

ideas.title: Self-Improving Scientific Ideation via Iterative RAG-Based Critique and Reranking
ideas.research_question: Can a PaperQA2-style agentic RAG system, when applied to evaluate and rerank its own generated hypotheses using multi-hop literature evidence, produce research ideas rated as more feasible and grounded than those from a single-pass overgenerate-and-rerank ideation agent?
ideas.mechanism: Use the modular tool decomposition from S2 (paper search, evidence gathering, answer synthesis) as the backbone for both idea generation and idea critique. Apply the overgenerate-and-rerank inference-time scaling from S3 to produce a large candidate set of research ideas, then route each candidate back through the PaperQA2 evidence-gathering pipeline (S1, S2) to score feasibility and contradictions against the literature. Rerank by a combined novelty-feasibility score.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Blind human expert ratings (novelty, feasibility, groundedness) comparing: (a) baseline overgenerate-and-rerank without RAG critique (S3 setting), (b) proposed RAG-critique reranking. Use 20 ideas per condition in a single domain (e.g., NLP or biochemistry). A statistically significant improvement in feasibility scores with non-degraded novelty constitutes a positive result.

ideas.title: PhD-Level Hypothesis Stress-Testing: Using Agentic RAG to Falsify LLM-Generated Research Ideas
ideas.research_question: Does applying a PaperQA2-style agentic literature search to actively seek disconfirming evidence for LLM-generated research ideas (S3) reduce the rate of ideas containing factual errors or already-refuted claims, as judged by domain experts?
ideas.mechanism: After an ideation agent (S3) generates and reranks candidate ideas, each top-ranked idea is passed to a PaperQA2 agent (S1, S2) configured in adversarial mode: the agent is prompted to search for prior work that contradicts, subsumes, or renders infeasible the proposed idea. The agent uses citation traversal and contextual summarization (S1, S2) to compile a falsification report. Ideas surviving adversarial review are surfaced to users with cited provenance.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Measure the proportion of surviving ideas containing factual errors or already-refuted claims, as annotated by PhD-level reviewers, comparing ideas with and without adversarial RAG filtering. A reduction in error rate of ≥20% in the filtered condition is the success threshold.

ideas.title: Scaling Ideation Quality via Retrieval Depth: Does More Evidence Improve Idea Novelty and Specificity?
ideas.research_question: Is there a measurable relationship between the number of RAG retrieval hops (controlled via the modular tool pipeline in S2) performed during idea generation (S3) and blind-rated novelty and specificity of the resulting ideas, as benchmarked against PhD expert performance (S1)?
ideas.mechanism: Instantiate the S2 modular RAG pipeline with variable retrieval depth (1-hop, 2-hop, 3-hop evidence gathering) as a controlled factor inside an ideation agent following the overgenerate-and-rerank strategy from S3. For each depth level, generate and rerank a fixed number of candidate ideas. Use the PhD-expert performance benchmark from S1 as a reference baseline for idea quality. Measure how retrieval depth affects idea ratings.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Collect blind expert ratings (novelty, specificity, actionability) for ideas generated at each retrieval depth across three topic domains. Test for monotonic improvement with depth using a rank correlation. Compare the best-depth condition against the PhD-level baseline from S1 to assess practical significance.

ideas.title: Mentor-Guided Open-Ended Discovery with Automated Peer Review
ideas.research_question: Does seeding an open-ended autonomous research loop (S1/S2) with a human mentor's baseline paper and codebase (S3) improve the acceptance rate of generated manuscripts under automated peer review compared to starting from scratch?
ideas.mechanism: Extend the S1/S2 open-ended pipeline so that iteration zero is bootstrapped from a mentor-provided baseline paper, LaTeX source, and codebase as in S3. The system identifies limitations (S3), generates improvement hypotheses, runs experiments autonomously (S1/S2), writes a manuscript, and evaluates it with the S1/S2 automated peer-review module. Multiple rounds of self-revision are allowed.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Run 20 trials each in mentor-seeded vs. scratch conditions on the same ML sub-domain. Compare automated peer-review scores and human expert ratings on a 5-point scale for novelty, correctness, and clarity. Report cost per paper (target <$15 per S2).

ideas.title: Iterative Limitation-Driven Idea Generation for Autonomous ML Research
ideas.research_question: Can explicitly surfacing a paper's limitations (S3) as structured prompts improve the quality and diversity of research ideas generated by a frontier LLM in an autonomous pipeline (S1/S2) relative to open-ended idea generation alone?
ideas.mechanism: Replace the free-form idea generation stage of S1/S2 with a two-step process: first apply S3's limitation-identification module to a seed paper to produce a structured list of gaps, then condition the S1/S2 idea-generation LLM on that list. The downstream stages (experiment design, execution on multi-file codebases via coding agents, manuscript writing, self-review) remain as in S1/S2/S3.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Generate 30 ideas under each condition (free-form vs. limitation-conditioned) for three seed papers. Score each idea on novelty, feasibility, and relevance using blinded human raters (3 raters, inter-rater agreement via Cohen's kappa). Measure fraction of ideas that survive automated self-review.

ideas.title: Cost-Calibrated Autonomous Research: Balancing Depth vs. Throughput
ideas.research_question: At fixed dollar budgets (e.g., $15, $50, $150 per paper), does allocating more compute to the limitation-identification and hypothesis-formulation phase (S3) or to the experiment-iteration phase (S1/S2) yield higher-quality autonomous research outputs?
ideas.mechanism: Implement a unified pipeline combining S3's mentor-guided limitation analysis and hypothesis formulation with S1/S2's experiment execution, visualization, manuscript writing, and automated peer review. Parameterize compute allocation as a ratio between the two phases and sweep across three budget levels. Track API costs per phase using exact usage logging.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: For each of three budget levels, run five allocation ratios (10/90, 25/75, 50/50, 75/25, 90/10 split between formulation and execution). Evaluate final manuscripts with automated peer-review scores (S1/S2 module) and one human expert per paper. Primary metric: peer-review score per dollar spent.

ideas.title: Aspect-Aware Novelty Gating for Agentic Ideation
ideas.research_question: Does inserting an aspect-based retrieval novelty-validation gate (S3) between the overgenerate and rerank stages of an LLM ideation pipeline (S2) improve the final rated novelty and feasibility of generated research ideas compared to reranking without such a gate?
ideas.mechanism: The S2 overgenerate-and-rerank pipeline produces a large candidate pool of research ideas. Before reranking, each candidate is passed to the S3 two-stage aspect-based retrieval pipeline, which checks whether the idea's core motivation and contribution aspects are already addressed in the literature; ideas flagged as fully answered (low novelty) are demoted or pruned. The surviving candidates are then reranked by the LLM judge. The S1 PaperQA2 agent provides the underlying literature retrieval and evidence summarization that feeds the S3 aspect decomposition step.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Ablation on a fixed set of NLP research prompts: compare (a) baseline S2 pipeline, (b) S2 with S3 novelty gate, and (c) S2 with S3 gate plus S1 evidence summarization. Human expert raters blind-score outputs on novelty and feasibility; measure the fraction of top-ranked ideas that are flagged as duplicating prior work by an independent literature search.

ideas.title: Unanswerable-Aware Scientific QA Benchmarking for Retrieval-Augmented Agents
ideas.research_question: Does augmenting a retrieval-augmented QA agent (S1) with an unanswerability detector derived from the S3 aspect-based pipeline reduce false-confident answers on scientific questions whose evidence is absent from the indexed corpus, while preserving accuracy on answerable questions?
ideas.mechanism: PaperQA2 (S1) currently retrieves and summarizes evidence but does not explicitly model the case where no retrieved article sufficiently addresses a question. The S3 pipeline's unanswerability signal—produced when aspect-level retrieval fails to cover a proposal's motivation—is adapted as a post-retrieval confidence calibration layer. The S2 inference-time scaling strategy (overgenerate candidate answers, rerank) is applied to the answer generation step so that the final answer selection is aware of evidence coverage scores, abstaining when coverage falls below a threshold.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Construct a benchmark of 200 scientific questions split evenly between answerable and unanswerable (evidence absent from the index). Measure F1 on answerable questions and abstention rate on unanswerable questions for (a) vanilla PaperQA2, (b) PaperQA2 with the S3 unanswerability layer, and (c) PaperQA2 with both S3 layer and S2 reranking. Target: abstention rate on unanswerable questions rises without degrading answerable F1.

ideas.title: Self-Validating Hypothesis Generation via Retrieval-Augmented Ideation and Evidence Auditing
ideas.research_question: Can a pipeline that couples LLM-driven overgeneration of scientific hypotheses (S2) with automated evidence auditing via a PhD-level retrieval agent (S1) and aspect-based novelty validation (S3) produce hypotheses that are simultaneously rated as novel by human experts and supported by retrievable evidence?
ideas.mechanism: Phase 1 uses the S2 overgenerate-and-rerank strategy to produce N candidate hypotheses for a target scientific domain. Phase 2 runs each hypothesis through the S3 two-stage aspect-based pipeline to decompose it into motivation and contribution aspects and retrieve supporting or refuting literature. Phase 3 uses the S1 PaperQA2 agent to perform deep evidence gathering and contextual summarization for the top-k hypotheses that survived Phase 2 novelty filtering. A final reranker scores hypotheses on the joint criterion of novelty (low S3 coverage of the exact claim) and evidential support (high S1 citation-backed plausibility for the underlying assumptions).
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Apply the pipeline to three scientific subfields. For the top-5 hypotheses per subfield, have domain experts rate novelty and evidential plausibility on a 5-point scale. Compare ratings against a baseline of pure S2 output (no S1/S3 validation) and against human-expert-written hypotheses. A positive result requires the pipeline's top-5 to score no lower than the S2 baseline on novelty and significantly higher on evidential plausibility.

ideas.title: Cross-Domain Automated Discovery: Applying ML-Optimized Research Pipelines to Health Informatics
ideas.research_question: Can an automated end-to-end research pipeline originally optimized for machine learning paper generation (as in S1/S2) be adapted to health informatics tasks (as in S3) while maintaining output quality above peer-review acceptance thresholds?
ideas.mechanism: Integrate the AI Scientist's idea generation and manuscript writing modules (S1) with OpenLens AI's specialized health informatics agents for literature review and data analysis (S3), then evaluate whether the combined pipeline produces health informatics manuscripts that meet the quality bar demonstrated for ML papers (S2).
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Run the hybrid pipeline on 5 standardized health informatics tasks (e.g., EHR analysis, clinical NLP); score outputs using the same automated peer-review mechanism from S1/S2; compare acceptance rates against the ML-domain baseline reported in S2.

ideas.title: Automated Meta-Review of AI-Generated Scientific Papers Across Domains
ideas.research_question: Does the automated peer-review component of the AI Scientist (S1) generalize reliably to health informatics manuscripts produced by OpenLens AI (S3), or does reviewer calibration degrade when applied outside the ML domain where its acceptance threshold was validated (S2)?
ideas.mechanism: Use the AI Scientist's automated reviewer (S1) to score a set of manuscripts: half generated by the AI Scientist itself in ML domains (S2) and half generated by OpenLens AI in health informatics (S3). Measure score distributions, inter-rater agreement with human reviewers, and domain-specific failure modes.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Collect 20 manuscripts per domain; compute correlation between automated reviewer scores and independent human expert scores; report whether the automated reviewer's calibration (validated in S2) degrades significantly on health informatics outputs from S3.

ideas.title: Modular Agent Specialization for Scientific Subdomain Depth vs. Breadth
ideas.research_question: Does decomposing the monolithic AI Scientist pipeline (S1) into domain-specialized modular agents—following the architecture of OpenLens AI (S3)—improve the rate at which generated ML papers exceed conference acceptance thresholds (S2) compared to the unmodified pipeline?
ideas.mechanism: Replace single-agent components in the AI Scientist (S1) with modular specialist agents mirroring OpenLens AI's architecture (S3)—separate agents for literature review, hypothesis generation, experiment design, and manuscript writing—then measure whether outputs more consistently surpass the acceptance threshold documented in S2.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Generate 30 ML papers each with the original AI Scientist pipeline and the modularized variant; apply the automated reviewer from S1/S2 to both sets; report acceptance rate difference and per-section quality scores to localize where modularization helps or hurts.

ideas.title: Self-Correcting AI Scientist via Reproducibility-Gated Iteration
ideas.research_question: Can integrating an automated reproducibility assessment module as a feedback gate within an end-to-end AI research pipeline reduce the rate of statistically irreproducible claims in generated manuscripts?
ideas.mechanism: Embed the agentic reproducibility pipeline (S2) as an internal review step within the AI Scientist framework (S1): after each experiment cycle, the reproducibility agent attempts to re-derive the focal statistical claims from raw outputs before the manuscript is finalized. Claims failing reproducibility trigger a re-run or revision loop. The Review-5k and Research-14k datasets (S3) are used to calibrate what claim types and writing patterns correlate with reproducibility failures, informing the reproducibility agent's focal claim extraction.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Generate 50 ML mini-papers using the baseline AI Scientist and 50 using the reproducibility-gated variant. Apply the S2 reproducibility pipeline post-hoc to both sets. Compare rates of successfully reproduced focal claims and human expert ratings of statistical soundness across the two conditions.

ideas.title: Benchmarking AI-Generated Research Quality Against Human Peer Review Standards Using Large-Scale Review Data
ideas.research_question: Do manuscripts produced by automated end-to-end research pipelines receive systematically different automated peer review scores compared to human-written papers, and can reproduciblity of their claims predict those score differences?
ideas.mechanism: Use the AI Scientist (S1) to generate a corpus of ML papers on benchmark tasks. Apply the S2 reproducibility pipeline to assess each paper's key statistical claims. Then score all papers — AI-generated and a matched sample from Research-14k (S3) — using the automated review model trained on Review-5k (S3). Correlate reproducibility scores (S2) with automated review scores (S3) to test whether reproducibility is a latent driver of review quality signals.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Produce 100 AI-generated papers (S1), run S2 reproducibility assessment on each, score all papers plus 100 matched human papers from Research-14k with a Review-5k-trained reviewer model. Report Spearman correlation between reproducibility rate and automated review score, and a Mann-Whitney test comparing score distributions of AI vs. human papers.

ideas.title: Training Reproducibility-Aware Peer Review Models Using Verified Claim Annotations
ideas.research_question: Does augmenting peer review training data with automated reproducibility verdicts improve a review model's ability to identify methodological weaknesses in submitted papers?
ideas.mechanism: Run the S2 reproducibility pipeline over the Research-14k corpus (S3) to annotate each paper's focal statistical claims as reproduced or not. Use these binary verdicts as auxiliary supervision signals when fine-tuning a review generation model on Review-5k (S3). The AI Scientist (S1) provides additional synthetic training papers with known ground-truth experimental outcomes, enabling controlled reproducibility labeling. Evaluate whether the augmented model better flags statistical and methodological weaknesses compared to a baseline trained on review text alone.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Fine-tune two review models on Review-5k: one baseline, one with reproducibility-label auxiliary loss derived from S2 annotations on Research-14k. Evaluate on a held-out set by measuring F1 for detecting papers flagged by human reviewers for statistical concerns, and compare mean review quality scores from a blinded human evaluation panel on 30 sample reviews per model.

ideas.title: Deficiency-Aware Meta-Review Generation with Rebuttal Grounding
ideas.research_question: Can fine-tuning an LLM on sentence-level deficiency annotations improve the factual grounding and deficiency coverage of generated meta-reviews compared to a baseline prompted with raw reviews?
ideas.mechanism: Use S1's sentence-level deficiency labels to construct a deficiency-extraction training signal, then train a meta-review generator on S3's large-scale rebuttal-aware review sequences (initial review → rebuttal → updated review → meta-review). Evaluate the resulting model on S2's 40 ICLR submissions using the existing 4,800 human judgments across five criteria to measure whether deficiency grounding improves meta-review quality.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Compare deficiency coverage (fraction of S1-labeled deficiency types surfaced) and S2 human-judgment scores (five criteria) between the deficiency-aware model and a GPT-4 baseline prompted with reviews only, across the 40 S2 submissions.

ideas.title: Rebuttal-Conditioned Review Quality Prediction
ideas.research_question: Do review deficiency patterns identified at submission time (S1) predict whether a reviewer will update their score after seeing the rebuttal (S3), and can this signal improve automated meta-review summarization quality (S2)?
ideas.mechanism: Map S1's deficiency label taxonomy onto the initial reviews in S3's multi-round corpus. Train a classifier to predict score changes between initial and updated reviews using deficiency features. Use predicted update-likelihood scores as soft weights when aggregating reviewer perspectives in a summarization model, then assess whether weighted summaries score higher on S2's five human-judgment criteria.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Measure Pearson correlation between predicted update-likelihood and actual score deltas in S3 held-out submissions; measure gain in S2 human-judgment scores for the weighted summarizer versus an unweighted baseline.

ideas.title: Longitudinal Calibration of LLM Meta-Reviewing Across Conference Years
ideas.research_question: Does LLM meta-review quality—measured against human judgments—degrade, improve, or remain stable as the target submissions span later ICLR years (2020–2023), and do deficiency patterns shift correspondingly?
ideas.mechanism: Use S3's year-stratified corpus (four ICLR years) to generate meta-reviews with the same LLM family used in S2, then score each generated meta-review with S2's five-criteria annotation rubric. Cross-reference systematic quality drops with S1's deficiency label distribution to identify which deficiency types drive year-over-year degradation. This reveals whether LLMs trained on static corpora become miscalibrated as review norms evolve.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Report S2-rubric scores per year stratum for LLM-generated meta-reviews on S3 submissions; compute correlation between year and each quality criterion; identify top-3 S1 deficiency types over-represented in low-scoring year strata.

ideas.title: Review-Calibrated Ideation: Using Peer Review Deficiency Signals to Guide LLM Research Hypothesis Generation
ideas.research_question: Can fine-tuning an LLM on ReviewCritique's deficiency-annotated reviews improve the feasibility ratings of its generated research ideas without sacrificing novelty?
ideas.mechanism: Use ReviewCritique (S1) deficiency labels as negative training signal — teaching the model which methodological, clarity, and scope weaknesses reviewers penalize — then fine-tune a hypothesis-generation model (analogous to S3's GPT-3 fine-tuning approach) on NLP literature. The hypothesis is that review-awareness closes the novelty-feasibility gap identified in S2 by steering generation away from patterns that attract feasibility critiques.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Generate 50 research ideas with the review-calibrated model and 50 with a baseline LLM. Have ≥10 NLP domain experts blind-rate each idea on novelty and feasibility (replicating the S2 protocol). Test whether the calibrated model closes the feasibility gap (S2) while maintaining novelty scores; compute inter-rater agreement.

ideas.title: Cross-Domain Feasibility Transfer: Applying NLP Review Annotations to Score Social-Science Hypotheses
ideas.research_question: Do deficiency categories derived from NLP peer reviews (S1) predict expert-rated feasibility weaknesses in social-psychology hypotheses generated by domain-fine-tuned LLMs (S3)?
ideas.mechanism: Extract a taxonomy of feasibility-related deficiency labels from ReviewCritique (S1). Apply this taxonomy as a zero-shot or few-shot classifier to hypotheses produced by a GPT-3 model fine-tuned on social psychology literature (S3). Compare classifier-flagged weaknesses against expert ratings collected in the S3 protocol, and against the novelty-vs-feasibility gap pattern observed in S2, to test whether review-derived signals transfer across scientific domains.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Take the hypothesis set from S3, run the deficiency classifier, and correlate deficiency flag rates with the expert scores already collected in S3. Report Spearman correlation between flagged feasibility deficiencies and expert feasibility ratings; compare effect sizes to S2's novelty–feasibility divergence.

ideas.title: Meta-Review Bootstrapping: Training LLM Meta-Reviewers on Deficiency Annotations to Rerank Novel-but-Risky Research Ideas
ideas.research_question: Can an LLM meta-reviewer trained on ReviewCritique sentence-level deficiency annotations reliably demote high-novelty but low-feasibility ideas surfaced by LLM ideation, without discarding genuinely strong candidates?
ideas.mechanism: Fine-tune a meta-reviewer on ReviewCritique (S1) deficiency labels and explanations to score draft ideas for specific weaknesses. Apply it as a reranking filter over a pool of LLM-generated ideas (reflecting the high-novelty, lower-feasibility profile in S2). Validate that the filter's feasibility judgments align with expert domain ratings by calibrating on the social-psychology hypothesis quality scores from S3 as an out-of-domain test set.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Generate 100 NLP research ideas with an LLM, rerank with the meta-reviewer, and present the top-20 reranked vs. top-20 unranked ideas to ≥10 expert raters blind to source. Measure whether reranked ideas show significantly higher feasibility scores (paired t-test) while retaining comparable novelty — using the S2 rating protocol as the evaluation template.

ideas.title: Calibrating LLM Review Quality Against Human Expert Annotations via Replication Judgment
ideas.research_question: Can an LLM judge trained on JudgeEval replication assessments better predict human-expert deficiency labels in ReviewCritique than a zero-shot LLM reviewer, and does calibrating on replication quality transfer to peer review quality estimation?
ideas.mechanism: Fine-tune or prompt-engineer an LLM judge using JudgeEval (S3) grading signals as a proxy for scientific rigor assessment, then evaluate that judge's ability to reproduce sentence-level deficiency annotations from ReviewCritique (S1). Use the novelty/feasibility trade-off observed in S2 as a covariate to test whether higher-novelty LLM-generated reviews are systematically harder for the judge to evaluate.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Measure agreement (Cohen's kappa) between the judge's deficiency labels and ReviewCritique expert annotations across LLM-generated vs. human-written reviews; compare against a zero-shot GPT-4 baseline. Report whether the replication-trained judge closes the gap on the harder LLM-generated review subset.

ideas.title: Using Peer Review Deficiency Labels to Diagnose Feasibility Gaps in LLM-Generated Research Ideas
ideas.research_question: Do the deficiency categories annotated in ReviewCritique systematically predict the feasibility deficit observed in LLM-generated ideas, and can a classifier trained on these labels flag low-feasibility ideas before human evaluation?
ideas.mechanism: Map ReviewCritique (S1) deficiency labels (e.g., missing baselines, unclear methodology) to feasibility-relevant dimensions identified in the S2 blind evaluation. Train a lightweight classifier on ReviewCritique annotations to score new LLM-generated research ideas for feasibility risk. Use JudgeEval (S3) replication success rates as an independent validity signal: ideas whose methodologies resemble successfully replicated work should receive higher feasibility scores.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: On a held-out set of LLM-generated ideas from the S2 evaluation protocol, compare classifier-predicted feasibility rankings against the human feasibility ratings reported in S2, measuring Spearman correlation. Validate that classifier scores align with JudgeEval replication outcomes on matched methodology types.

ideas.title: Meta-Review Consistency Across the Idea-to-Replication Pipeline
ideas.research_question: Is an LLM meta-reviewer that is benchmarked on ReviewCritique consistent in its quality judgments when applied sequentially to the same scientific contribution at the ideation stage (S2), the submission review stage (S1), and the replication stage (S3)?
ideas.mechanism: Apply a single LLM meta-reviewer pipeline to all three stages: score raw research ideas using the novelty/feasibility rubric from S2, score paper submissions using ReviewCritique (S1) deficiency taxonomy, and score replication submissions using JudgeEval (S3) criteria. Measure rank-order consistency of quality assessments across stages for matched topics, testing whether the LLM's evaluation behavior is stable or systematically shifts by pipeline stage.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Compute Kendall's tau between LLM quality rankings at each stage pair (ideation vs. submission, submission vs. replication) on a set of at least 20 topics traceable across datasets. Report whether stage-specific calibration (training the meta-reviewer on each dataset separately) improves consistency relative to a single zero-shot prompt.

ideas.title: Domain-Specialized Tool Augmentation for Scientific Reproducibility Agents
ideas.research_question: Does equipping a task-specialized reproducibility agent (analogous to CORE-Agent) with a curated domain-specific tool library (analogous to ToolUniverse) yield measurably higher accuracy on social science reproducibility tasks compared to the tool-free baseline?
ideas.mechanism: Extend the CORE-Agent architecture (S2) with a structured tool registry covering statistical re-analysis, dataset retrieval, and code execution, mirroring how ToolUniverse provides modular capabilities to discovery agents (S3). The enriched agent is then evaluated on the same four-class reproducibility scoring benchmark used in S1/S2.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Compare four-class accuracy of baseline CORE-Agent (~21%, S1/S2) against the tool-augmented variant on the same held-out benchmark; a statistically significant improvement above the random-guess baseline (~25%) would support the hypothesis.

ideas.title: Reproducibility-Guided Hypothesis Filtering in Therapeutic Discovery Pipelines
ideas.research_question: Can embedding an automated reproducibility-assessment module—modeled on the CORE-Agent evaluation framework—into an end-to-end therapeutic discovery pipeline (like the ToolUniverse approach) reduce the propagation of findings from irreproducible preclinical studies into downstream drug candidate generation?
ideas.mechanism: Insert a reproducibility-scoring agent (S1, S2) as a pre-filter stage before the therapeutic discovery agent (S3) consumes literature-derived hypotheses. Candidates sourced from studies scored as low-reproducibility are flagged or deprioritized, while the discovery agent proceeds normally for high-reproducibility inputs.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: In a controlled case study (e.g., hypercholesterolemia as in S3), compare the predicted-property profiles of drug analogs generated from filtered vs. unfiltered literature inputs; measure the fraction of top candidates that trace to high- vs. low-reproducibility sources.

ideas.title: Benchmark Transfer: Adapting End-to-End Discovery Evaluation to Social Science Reproducibility
ideas.research_question: Can the end-to-end outcome-based evaluation methodology used to assess therapeutic discovery agents (S3) be adapted to produce a more informative benchmark for social science reproducibility agents than the current four-class accuracy metric, which leaves state-of-the-art agents near random chance (S1)?
ideas.mechanism: Reframe reproducibility assessment as a sequential decision task—mirroring the multi-step tool-use pipeline in S3—where intermediate agent actions (data retrieval, statistical re-execution, result comparison) are scored individually in addition to final classification. Apply targeted agent specialization lessons from S2 to construct a baseline agent for this richer benchmark.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Implement the step-level benchmark on a subset of the existing S1 corpus; measure whether step-level scores correlate with final four-class labels and whether the new metric better differentiates agent variants than the near-floor four-class accuracy reported in S1/S2.

ideas.title: Reproducibility-Aware Drug Discovery Agents
ideas.research_question: Can augmenting therapeutic discovery agents with reproducibility-scoring feedback (analogous to social science reproducibility assessment) reduce the rate of non-replicable intermediate findings in end-to-end drug analog identification pipelines?
ideas.mechanism: Extend the ToolUniverse agentic framework (S2) with a reproducibility-assessment module inspired by the rubric used to score social science agents (S1). At each reasoning step, the agent self-scores its intermediate hypotheses on a reproducibility rubric before committing to a tool call. LLM-generated hypotheses about drug candidates (S3) are then filtered or ranked by reproducibility score prior to experimental validation.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Run the hypercholesterolemia case study (S2) with and without the reproducibility filter. Compare the fraction of intermediate candidate hypotheses that survive an independent replication check (wet-lab or in-silico re-run) between the two conditions across 20 candidate analogs.

ideas.title: Benchmarking LLM Hypothesis Quality via Social-Science Reproducibility Metrics
ideas.research_question: Do LLM-generated scientific hypotheses that score higher on social-science reproducibility criteria (S1) also produce algorithms that more reliably outperform baselines when experimentally validated (S3)?
ideas.mechanism: Use the four-class reproducibility scoring framework from S1 as a proxy quality signal for hypotheses generated by LLMs (S3). Apply this scoring to a set of LLM-generated data-science algorithm hypotheses before running end-to-end experimental validation. Correlate reproducibility scores with downstream benchmark outperformance rates. Optionally, integrate ToolUniverse-style agentic tooling (S2) to automate hypothesis scoring and experimental execution.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Generate 30 LLM hypotheses for algorithm improvements on a held-out data science task. Have human raters and the automated agent (S1-style) score reproducibility. Run experimental validation (S3-style). Compute Spearman correlation between reproducibility score and whether the resulting algorithm beats the baseline.

ideas.title: Self-Correcting Agentic Science Pipelines with Hypothesis Validation Loops
ideas.research_question: Can an end-to-end agentic pipeline that combines tool-augmented discovery (S2), automated hypothesis generation and validation (S3), and iterative reproducibility self-assessment (S1) achieve above-random accuracy on cross-domain scientific reproducibility tasks where current agents fail?
ideas.mechanism: Construct a multi-phase agent: phase 1 uses ToolUniverse-style tools (S2) to gather domain evidence; phase 2 uses LLM hypothesis generation with experimental validation loops (S3) to propose and test candidate conclusions; phase 3 applies the reproducibility scoring rubric (S1) to the agent's own outputs, triggering re-investigation when reproducibility score falls below a threshold. The loop continues until a confidence criterion is met or a budget is exhausted.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Evaluate the pipeline on the same four-class social science reproducibility benchmark used in S1, comparing accuracy against the 21.4% CORE-Agent baseline. Report accuracy, mean number of self-correction loops, and token cost per task over a 50-item held-out split.

ideas.title: Agentic Hypothesis-to-Reproduction Pipeline for Social Science
ideas.research_question: Can an agentic system that generates and validates algorithmic hypotheses (as in S3) improve end-to-end reproducibility assessment accuracy in social science beyond the 21.4% ceiling reported for CORE-Agent (S1)?
ideas.mechanism: Extend the LLM hypothesis-generation loop from S3 to social science reproducibility tasks: the agent generates candidate analysis scripts from paper descriptions, executes them via a ToolUniverse-style tool layer (S2), and scores outputs against reported results. The hypothesis-generation step replaces brittle fixed pipelines that caused CORE-Agent's near-random performance (S1).
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Re-run the same four-class reproducibility benchmark used in S1 with the new pipeline and compare accuracy against the 21.4% CORE-Agent baseline and the random-guessing floor. A statistically significant improvement on held-out papers constitutes a positive result.

ideas.title: Tool-Augmented Scientific Hypothesis Validation for Drug Discovery
ideas.research_question: Does grounding LLM-generated algorithmic hypotheses (S3) in domain-specific wet-lab and cheminformatics tools via a ToolUniverse-style interface (S2) yield drug candidates with better predicted ADMET profiles than hypotheses validated only in silico without tool augmentation?
ideas.mechanism: Use the LLM hypothesis loop from S3 to propose structural modifications to known drug scaffolds; route each hypothesis through ToolUniverse tools (S2) for docking, ADMET prediction, and synthesis feasibility checks. The reproducibility-scoring insight from S1 motivates rigorous, structured evaluation criteria so that claimed improvements are independently verifiable rather than anecdotal.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: On the hypercholesterolemia case study from S2, compare the top-ranked analog produced by tool-augmented hypothesis generation against the analog reported in S2 on predicted LDL-lowering potency, toxicity flags, and synthetic accessibility score. A win on at least two of three metrics is the success criterion.

ideas.title: Benchmarking Agentic Science Systems with Reproducibility-Aware Scoring
ideas.research_question: Can a reproducibility-grounded evaluation framework (informed by the failure modes in S1) reveal whether LLM hypothesis-generation agents (S3) and tool-augmented discovery agents (S2) produce genuinely reproducible results or merely locally plausible ones?
ideas.mechanism: Construct a cross-domain benchmark (social science from S1, data science from S3, therapeutic discovery from S2) where each agent output is scored using the same four-class reproducibility rubric from S1. Agents are tested both with (S2-style) and without structured tool access to isolate the contribution of tool grounding to reproducibility. Hypothesis-generation quality from S3 is measured by whether downstream agents can reproduce the flagged winning algorithms from held-out descriptions.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Report four-class reproducibility accuracy for each agent-domain combination. A meaningful result is any condition that exceeds the 21.4% CORE-Agent ceiling from S1 on at least one domain, with error analysis identifying which failure modes (execution, interpretation, scoring) dominate.

ideas.title: Self-Verifying Replication Agents with Dynamic Compute Allocation
ideas.research_question: Can a multi-agent scientific replication system that uses self-verification during each sequential replication task (document analysis, literature review, data acquisition, code generation) outperform a fixed-budget replication pipeline in terms of methodological fidelity and reproducibility rate?
ideas.mechanism: Combine S3's sequential decomposition pipeline (document analysis → literature review → data acquisition → code generation) with S2's verifier-guided test-time scaling, where each specialized agent serves as its own verifier at each stage, and use S1's asynchronous resource allocation framework to dynamically assign more compute to stages where self-verification signals high uncertainty or failure.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Select 20 published ML papers with available code. Run the pipeline with and without self-verification and dynamic compute scaling. Measure: (1) code execution success rate, (2) numeric result match within 5% tolerance, (3) total tool-call budget consumed per paper.

ideas.title: Budget-Adaptive Parallel Literature Synthesis via Asynchronous Verification
ideas.research_question: Does asynchronous parallel execution of literature review subtasks, governed by a shared tool-call budget and self-verification signals, reduce wall-clock time and improve claim accuracy compared to sequential literature review in scientific replication workflows?
ideas.mechanism: Within S3's literature review stage, deploy multiple specialized LLM agents in parallel using S1's asynchronous task execution framework. Each agent applies S2's self-verifier strategy to assess confidence in retrieved claims under a controlled tool-call budget, with S1's resource allocator redistributing budget from high-confidence agents to low-confidence ones in real time.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Run literature review on 30 systematic review topics. Compare parallel self-verifying agents (this approach) vs. single sequential agent on: (1) recall of ground-truth key citations, (2) hallucination rate of cited findings, (3) wall-clock time to completion.

ideas.title: Difficulty-Tiered Compute Scheduling for Multi-Stage Scientific Reasoning
ideas.research_question: Can routing scientific replication subtasks to different tiers of test-time compute—determined by a self-verification confidence score—improve overall replication quality relative to uniform compute allocation across all stages?
ideas.mechanism: Use S3's four-stage replication decomposition as the task structure. After each stage completes, the agent applies S2's self-verification loop to produce a confidence score. S1's dynamic scaling framework then maps low-confidence scores to extended reasoning budgets and high-confidence scores to reduced budgets, enabling adaptive allocation without a separate verifier model.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Replicate 15 computational biology papers. Compare three conditions: (a) uniform budget per stage, (b) difficulty-tiered budget via self-verification, (c) maximum budget throughout. Measure replication success rate and total compute cost (tool calls) to compute a quality-per-cost efficiency metric.

ideas.title: Self-Verifying Hypothesis Prioritization via Asynchronous Multi-Agent Scaling
ideas.research_question: Can a multi-agent hypothesis-generation system that uses the agent itself as an inline verifier—without a separate verifier model—dynamically reallocate tool-call budgets across agents to improve hypothesis quality on benchmark scientific discovery tasks?
ideas.mechanism: Using the asynchronous task execution framework (S1, S2), spawn parallel hypothesis-generation agents that each apply self-verifying test-time scaling (S3): after initial hypothesis generation, the same agent re-examines its output under a controlled tool-call budget and scores confidence. The orchestrator then reallocates compute (additional tool-call budget) to agents whose self-assessed confidence is lowest, iteratively refining the weakest hypotheses rather than uniformly scaling all agents.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Run on a fixed scientific QA benchmark (e.g., SciQ or a subset of literature-grounded tasks). Compare hypothesis acceptance rate and factual consistency between (a) uniform compute allocation with no self-verification, (b) self-verification with fixed budgets (S3 alone), and (c) the proposed adaptive reallocation scheme (S1+S2+S3). Measure quality via held-out judge model scoring across at least 100 questions.

ideas.title: Budget-Aware Asynchronous Scaling for Long-Horizon Scientific Reasoning Pipelines
ideas.research_question: Does allocating test-time tool-call budget adaptively across pipeline stages—guided by per-stage self-verification signals—improve end-to-end correctness on multi-step scientific reasoning tasks compared to static per-stage budgets?
ideas.mechanism: Structure a scientific reasoning pipeline (literature retrieval → hypothesis formation → experimental design) as asynchronous agents (S1, S2). At each stage, the active agent acts as its own verifier (S3): it audits its intermediate output and emits a difficulty score. The orchestration layer reads these signals and dynamically reassigns unused budget from low-difficulty stages to high-difficulty ones before the next stage begins, without requiring a separate verifier model.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Construct a three-stage pipeline on a structured scientific reasoning task (e.g., drug-repurposing hypothesis chains). Measure final-answer accuracy and total tool calls consumed under (a) equal static budget per stage, (b) self-verification within each stage but no cross-stage reallocation, and (c) full adaptive cross-stage reallocation. Report accuracy vs. budget curves across at least three total-budget levels.

ideas.title: Difficulty-Stratified Compute Allocation for Ensemble Hypothesis Generation
ideas.research_question: If a self-verifying agent (acting as its own verifier) classifies generated hypotheses by difficulty before ensemble aggregation, does routing harder hypotheses to additional asynchronous agents with expanded tool-call budgets improve recall of correct hypotheses relative to a flat ensemble?
ideas.mechanism: An initial agent generates a candidate hypothesis set and applies self-verifying inference (S3) to label each hypothesis as easy, medium, or hard based on internal confidence after a base tool-call budget. The asynchronous orchestration framework (S1, S2) then spawns additional agents only for hard-labeled hypotheses, each running extended reasoning under an enlarged budget, while easy hypotheses are passed through directly. Final outputs are aggregated across all agents.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Evaluate on a scientific hypothesis-recall task where ground-truth correct hypotheses are known (e.g., a held-out subset of a biomedical literature dataset). Compare recall@K and compute cost between (a) flat ensemble of N agents with equal budgets, (b) single agent with self-verification only, and (c) the proposed difficulty-stratified routing. Vary K and report the Pareto frontier of recall vs. total tool calls.

ideas.title: Iterative Self-Verifying Multi-Agent Scaling for Biomedical Reasoning
ideas.research_question: Does combining self-verification during inference (S2) with iterative multi-trial accumulation (S3) inside an asynchronously scheduled multi-agent framework (S1) yield greater accuracy gains on biomedical benchmarks than either scaling strategy alone?
ideas.mechanism: A multi-agent system (S1) orchestrates parallel reasoning chains on biomedical questions; each agent acts as its own verifier under a tool-call budget (S2); completed trials feed accumulated reasoning traces back into subsequent iterations (S3), with the asynchronous scheduler dynamically allocating more compute to questions where self-verification confidence remains low.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Run the combined system on HLE: Biomedicine across 1, 3, and 5 iterative trials, comparing accuracy to (a) single-pass multi-agent baseline, (b) self-verifying agent without iteration, and (c) iterative system without self-verification, measuring accuracy and total tool-call cost at each condition.

ideas.title: Budget-Aware Adaptive Compute Allocation Across Iterative Reasoning Trials
ideas.research_question: Can an asynchronous task scheduler (S1) that monitors per-question self-verification confidence signals (S2) across iterative trials (S3) reduce total compute cost while preserving accuracy gains, by reallocating budget from already-solved questions to persistently hard ones?
ideas.mechanism: After each iterative trial (S3), the multi-agent scheduler (S1) collects the verifier confidence score produced by self-verification (S2) for each question; questions exceeding a confidence threshold are retired while remaining budget is redistributed to low-confidence questions in the next trial, creating a dynamic anytime-compute profile.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Compare accuracy vs. total tool-calls on HLE: Biomedicine between fixed-budget uniform allocation and confidence-guided reallocation across 5 trials, measuring (a) accuracy at matched budgets and (b) budget required to reach 26% accuracy from S3.

ideas.title: Self-Verifying Iterative Multi-Agent Transfer Across Scientific Domains
ideas.research_question: Do the iterative accuracy gains demonstrated in biomedicine (S3) transfer to other scientific domains (e.g., chemistry, physics) when the system uses self-verification under budget constraints (S2) inside a dynamically scaling multi-agent architecture (S1), or are the gains domain-specific?
ideas.mechanism: The asynchronous multi-agent framework (S1) is applied to domain-specific benchmarks; within each trial the agent verifies its own outputs under a controlled tool-call budget (S2); trials are run iteratively accumulating reasoning experience (S3); accuracy trajectories across domains are compared to isolate whether iterative self-verifying scaling is a general property or tied to biomedical task structure.
ideas.minimal_evaluation: Run 5 iterative trials on at least two non-biomedical scientific benchmarks (e.g., GPQA Chemistry, SciBench Physics), reporting per-domain accuracy curves and comparing slope of improvement to the 14%→26% trajectory from S3, with matched compute budgets across domains.
